newsitem.title: FRANCE: France pledges to promote euro zone council.
newsitem.headline: France pledges to promote euro zone council.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis pledged on Tuesday to use the months ahead to promote France's idea of setting up an economic council to co-ordinate policies among countries inside European monetary union.
"This stability and growth council will be an absolute necessity," he told a New Year ceremony for the press.
"In the months ahead we will seek even more support for the idea of giving Europe a stability and growth council. It is an idea which is making progress," he said.
France has said its wants an informal council -- meeting at the level of finance ministers or heads of state and government -- to counterbalance the future European Central Bank.
It would have a similar structure to the informal Group of Seven (G7) rich nations forum -- another grouping first set up by France -- which has no secretariat nor headquarters.

The idea has run into opposition from those who fear that France might use it to push for a depreciation in the euro against the dollar, or to put pressure on the future European Central Bank when fixing monetary policy.
Bundesbank council member Olaf Sievert on Tuesday dismissed the proposed stability council as meaningless.

"Of course, once the European Central Bank has the power to take the role which the Maastricht Treaties have given it, there may be some comfort in the fact that a stability council, which has nothing to decide, would only make a fool of itself if it hit on the idea of suggesting that the moon should go in the oposite direction from that which is ordained," he said.
"But why then bother with such a council at all?" he said, according to a speech prepared for delivery to a reception in the eastern German city of Leipzig.

French official sources say the aim would be to use the council to discuss fiscal policies and the implementation of a budget stability pact agreed last December obliging governments to limit budget deficits after the launch of the euro in 1999.

It would also discuss exchange rates, agreeing a common position on the euro for the bigger countries representing Europe at the G7, or co-ordinating links between the euro and currencies of European countries outside the single currency.
Under the Maastricht treaty, exchange rate policy will remain in the hands of governments after the launch of the euro while the independent central bank will fix monetary policy.
Despite resistance, officials in France and abroad say the idea of an "economic government", first proposed by late finance minister Pierre Beregovoy, is gaining support.

"The French idea, in fact was supported by Germany, by Belgium, by Luxembourg and by others," Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television earlier this week.
One European diplomat has suggested Germany had promised backing for euro zone economic summits in return for French acceptance of the budget stability pact.
